attribution: Part of the Mahabharata (Bhishma Parva); traditionally attributed to Vyasa
author: vyasa
period: Scholars commonly place its composition between roughly the 5th and 2nd centuries BCE, with some proposing later layers; traditionally set at the start of the Kurukshetra war
summary: A 700-verse dialogue in which Krishna counsels the warrior Arjuna, who has collapsed in despair on the battlefield, on action, the Self and devotion.
whyRead: The Gita is one of the most widely read and commented-on texts in Indian thought, and it brings together threads from the Upanishads, Sankhya, Yoga and devotional religion in a single conversation. It is also the one primary source fully available in this app: all 700 verses with Swami Ramsukhdas's Sadhak Sanjivani commentary, so you can read any verse cited elsewhere.
story: On the eve of the Kurukshetra war, Arjuna asks his charioteer Krishna to drive between the two armies. Seeing teachers, relatives and friends on the opposing side, he refuses to fight. Krishna's response, spread over eighteen chapters, moves from the immortality of the Self to disciplined action, meditation, the nature of God, a vision of Krishna's cosmic form, and finally surrender; at the end Arjuna says his confusion is gone. The dialogue is framed as Sanjaya's report to the blind king Dhritarashtra.
questions: How should I act when every choice seems to cause harm?
What in me does not die?
Can one act without being bound by the results?
What is the relation between knowledge, action and devotion?

keyTeachings.title: The Self is not born and does not die
keyTeachings.text: Krishna begins by distinguishing the unchanging Self from the changing body. Grief over death, the text argues, comes from identifying with what is perishable.

keyTeachings.title: Act without attachment to results
keyTeachings.text: A central teaching is that one has a claim on action but not on its fruits. Action done as duty and offering, without craving for outcomes, is said not to bind.

keyTeachings.title: Equanimity is itself yoga
keyTeachings.text: The Gita repeatedly defines yoga as evenness of mind in success and failure, pleasure and pain. Its portrait of the person of steady wisdom (sthitaprajna) is a model of this.

keyTeachings.title: Several paths, one goal
keyTeachings.text: The text discusses the disciplines of action (karma), knowledge (jnana), meditation (dhyana) and devotion (bhakti). Commentators disagree about how these relate: Shankara emphasises knowledge, Ramanuja devotion, and many modern readers see an integration.

keyTeachings.title: The three gunas
keyTeachings.text: Drawing on Sankhya, the Gita analyses nature (prakriti) into three qualities, sattva, rajas and tamas, and uses them to classify food, faith, charity, knowledge and character.

keyTeachings.title: Surrender to God
keyTeachings.text: In its closing teaching Krishna invites Arjuna to take refuge in him alone. Devotional traditions treat this as the culmination of the text.
